#8431. Te Araroa day 22: Auckland here we come!

27.5km, Mangawhai trail host to Pakiri Paradise

Most of us (me, Lindsay, Sinead, Annabel and Anica) got going at around 7am again, although this time with good reason as we were expecting a bit of a longer day and needed to make a tidal river crossing later. The place we were staying was run by people who had previously done TA and provided everything hikers could need, at the very reasonable price of $10 per night. It was a great place to stay, and we walked out of the gate practically right back onto trail. We had been talking about coffee, but didn’t think that anything would be open at that time. But luck was on our side! Literally 50 metres down the street there was a coffee and smoothie van. What a great start to the day. While I was at university I was very much fuelled by coffee, but since then I’ve mostly switched to decaf. But I have been enjoying drinking it again while I’ve been hiking – it gives me a great energy boost, which puts me in a good mood, and I think the negative side effects I’ve experienced previously are reduced by having physical activity to funnel that energy into.

I found a friend when I went to pack away my tent

Coffee obtained, it was going to be a good morning!

Unfortunately, the day started with a decent road walk of about 7km, which I don’t think any of us had quite registered was coming. Eventually we made it to the beach we would be walking along for the greater part of the day. The signage was familiar to me and I didn’t quite realise why until I registered that it was Auckland Council signage. We had made it to Auckland region! The Northland/Auckland boundary is just south of Mangawhai so that morning, we had completed the first region of Te Araroa. Northland is one of the longest (perhaps the longest?) regions on TA, owing to its long and thin geography. So this was a significant milestone. It was also probably the region I was least looking forward to, yet I loved it. Not every minute, of course, but distance had made my heart grow fonder and I was able to appreciate the beauty of the place with fresh eyes.

The beach looked pleasingly short when we got onto it. That is, until I realised that the headland I could see was not the end of the beach section, but just a blip a few kilometres in. Still, the first section went pretty quickly and soon we were approaching the headland. There were hoards of surfers and foil board surfers, which looked pretty cool! There was also an interesting set up on the beach. Evidently a photoshoot was going on – a bed was set up, and a model posed on it in pajamas while a drone hovered and various involved people fluttered around. I’m sure the six dirty hikers walking through the background didn’t improve their shots!

The first part of the beach, looking towards Te Arai point

Up on Te Arai Point, there were awesome views along the coast. The tracks weren’t super well-marked though, and the route was a bit un-intuitive. I was with Lindsay and Sinead at this point, and eventually we reached a wooded section that popped out on a road back to the beach. Just before the road we stumbled (almost literally) upon Zoe, who was taking a break in what she pointed out might be the last shade for a while. We plopped down to join her, and collectively decided that the rest of the beach necessitated podcasts. I realised I had forgotten to download more episodes when I last had wifi, and scrambled around for something to listen to. I tried an audiobook but I wasn’t really getting into it, and stopped to switch to music and try to find the specific song I had in my head that morning (u + me = <3 by Olivia Rodrigo, in case you were wondering). Tunes acquired, I set off again.

This beach was actually perhaps the most annoying we have had to walk down so far. The tide was fully in at this point and the available area to walk on was soft, slopey, and narrow in places. There was one spot where the waves had created a bit of a cliff about 75cm tall, with very little space between the top of the cliff and the dunes behind. My feet were already wet from a stream crossing earlier, so I just decided to commit and walk in the water below the cliff. Apparently some of the others had taken their chances with the top of the cliff, with fairly unsuccessful results. It was a shame they were behind me, as the descriptions they gave of their falls were pretty amusing!

Walking over Te Arai point, with the surfers in the background

The other notable thing about the beach was the number of dead birds we came across. I really haven’t seen that many before. I hope it isn’t bird flu, which has recently arrived in NZ – perhaps it’s just something to do with the ocean currents that lots of dead stuff washes up there?

At about 11:45 I was hungry. I was going to grab a snack and keep going, but realised I might as well stop for lunch. Who says lunch can’t happen before 12, anyway? I was hungry so I might as well eat properly. I enjoyed my wraps with fresh salad, although I kept dropping things that then got covered in sand. Annabel had told me about these sun-dried tomatoes that come without oil, and I had bought some in Mangawhai. They were great, 10/10 reccommend those. While I was lunching, the others all passed me. After a few more kilometres of walking, I came across everyone sat on the beach eating their (late) lunch. We were nearly at the tidal estuary, which the trail notes said could be crossed 90 minutes either side of low tide. It was 2pm, and low tide wasn’t until nearly 5. But the others reckoned someone else had crossed outside of the reccommended window, and we decided to go and have a look.

The butterflies were having a good dance in my stomach as we approached the estuary. I find rivers quite scary, especially when I don’t know how deep they’ll be. We went to the mouth, as that’s where the smaller streams on the beach had been shallowest. But the water here looked quite fast-flowing, so we went further up to a wider, slower bend. It was impossible to tell how deep it was, but at least we wouldn’t get swept away. Sinéad offered to be the guinea pig. She went up to her ankles, then her knees – and then she was basically across. No problem! We all followed without difficulty. Sometimes the trail notes really overstate the difficulty of a thing. I guess it can be deeper sometimes – but we crossed 3 hours before low tide with no bother, when the notes suggested 90 minutes. One of the most valuable pieces of advice I got about TA, which I tell to everyone, came from a couple of NOBO hikers that I picked up near Nelson Lakes last season. They said that there is a lot of scare-mongering from other hikers, but you have to see for yourself and not put too much stock in what everyone else is saying. And apparently the same goes for the trail notes, too!

The crossing was so fine! Zoe wading across with me, Lindsay, Annabel and Anica waiting. Photo by Sinéad

Putting shoes and socks back on after the beach

We walked up the beach towards a holiday park. We were planning to go a bit further for the day but hoped they would sell us some cold drinks, and maybe fill some water bottles. It was a bit unclear where to go, but there was a man mowing the grass. ‘You lot look like an invading army!’ he called down to us. I suppose the six of us did look like we were plotting how to storm the castle! He invited us to come through the campground and rinse out our shoes and socks. After my sandpaper socks the other day, this was a very welcome invitation. He also said that the notes don’t give good advice about where to cross the river we had just been over. It’s much shallower inland, but the area is home to rare nesting birds, so DOC won’t allow the TA trust to tell people to cross further inland. Personally, I’m happy to wait a bit for the tides if it means not disturbing the birds. But I can see that it’s frustrating for the locals to see people being given less-good safety advice.

After washing our feet, we all headed over to the shop where we bought ice creams and cold drinks, and checked out the next bit of the route. Everyone kept saying it was really steep, but for some reason I didn’t think it looked too bad on the map. Then I decided to look at a different map app, the one I normally use, and the contour lines looked way denser! I realised that the contours on the TA app are really light and narrow compared to the ones on the map I’m used to, so things don’t look as steep. I guess that could be helpful, in some ways.

After a while, we headed off down the road. It was a fairly quiet road, and it wasn’t too long before we reached some track. The hill began immediately, and it was steep but not impossible. I ended up passing the others at the first flattish bit and continued on up. The views were pretty good and I felt happy about my fitness. I had a full 4 day resupply on my back but I found the hill ok, and I was able to keep plugging on without having to stop too often. Towards the top, there was a large fallen tree that I had to scramble over. Then I realised I was at the turn off for where we would be staying, and stopped to wait for the others. I watched them all clamber over the tree with varying levels of elegance. I would have taken photos but I didn’t want to walk back down the hill.

You can just see the others lower down the hill

The house we were staying at was a couple of hundred metres along a side-track. Annabel and I got there first, and the couple came out and introduced themselves, and asked where we were from. Annabel is also from southern England, to which the guy responded that we were both ‘bloody Southerners’; he’s from Yorkshire! The rest of the group arrived and they showed us where we could pitch our tents. It wasn’t as luxurious as the previous night, but we had everything we needed. And, they showed us the view of Auckland city from their garden! This was the first time we had seen the city, and although it still looked very far away, it was cool to know we were getting closer. Everyone was planning to take some time off or visit friends in Auckland, and it’s also the first major city on the route. So it seems to have become a big milestone in everyone’s minds.

You can’t see it, but trust me when I say that the Auckland city skyline was visible in this view

The weather was threatening rain so we pitched our tents, which were soaked from the morning dew still. I managed to snag a decent spot, but some of the others were less lucky and Annabel realised she had pitched her tent in a bit of a bog. Our hosts came out with a packet of scorched almonds, which was very nice of them! A little while later, Xavier showed up. He was at the campsite the previous night, but I didn’t end up speaking to him. Some of the others knew him from before, but I hadn’t met him so I took the chance to introduce myself. Then we carefully prepared dinner on the tables and chairs that kept sinking into the mud, and sat around talking for a while before calling it a night.

#8428. Why the Post-Rut Is Actually the Best Time to Hunt Whitetails

Published Nov 13, 2026 3:39 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

A few years ago in North Dakota, the entire month of November was warm, with hardly any snow. “Needless to say, the rut was tough,” says resident bowhunter Derek Plautz.

Plautz hunted hard for weeks without seeing a shooter buck. But in early December, the weather cooled down, snow flew, and the deer started moving. With two days left in the season, Plautz checked his trail camera. Finally, a big 10-point.

He didn’t have a tree stand in the area, so he built a little brush blind behind a fallen tree and climbed in for the evening hunt. Deer started moving and soon here came Big Ten, bronze antlers glinting in the fading light. When the buck crossed at 30 yards, Derek let fly. The deer kicked like a mule and ran, but it didn’t go far.

“What a great way to end a weird season,” Derek says. “I got to hunt for weeks and then cap it off with a big buck at the very end!”

A hunt like Derek’s is becoming the norm rather than the exception across North America. My observation and theory: As temperatures have gotten warmer in late October and November, deer patterns are gradually changing. While does and bucks still breed in mid-November as they always have, they tend to move less in daylight and more during cooler nights.

In December, it starts to cool down for longer stretches at a time—for days or weeks—and deer start moving with more vigor. Bucks are still rutty, prowling, and looking for the last receptive does of the year.

Each year I hunt in several states in early to mid-December, from Kansas to Oklahoma to Virginia. I am witnessing good to great deer movement, and more late rutting activity than ever before. Such good activity, in fact, that the early post-rut is becoming my most productive time to hunt.

One of the country’s top whitetail hunters agrees. “The weeks following the rut are my favorite time without a doubt,” says Midwestern hunter and Outdoor Channel personality Mark Drury. “I see more mature bucks in the post-rut period beginning in early December than at any other time of year. Big bucks are on the hunt for food and the last does.” Here are some ways to capitalize.

Your strategy from early December through the end of the season should center around the limited food sources that remain for deer. Both does and bucks are run down from the primary rut, and they have to eat. The colder (and snowier) it is in December, the harder deer move to and from the feed, and the more visible they will be in daylight.

You’ll see the most animals if you have access to corn and soybeans, or alfalfa in the West. A patch of standing corn is especially good, as it provides both eats and cover for deer.

In a harvested bean field, scout edges and corners where a few strips of standing beans were missed by harvest. Those will be a magnet for deer. One chilly December evening, I killed one of my biggest Iowa bucks, a 150-inch 10-point, by finding a few leftover beans and taking a ground setup nearby.

The less gun pressure in and around a field during the hunting season, the more bucks you will see active in daylight. Pray for snow and temps from the teens to mid-30s. A hungry buck might pop out into the crops morning or afternoon, or even briefly in the middle of the day. Bundle up and be out there till the end.

If you hunt big woods, public or private, miles from the nearest crops, you won’t see nearly as many deer, none some days. To have a chance of punching your buck tag you must find and watch what little food/cover mix is left for a buck: greenery on the edge of a clear-cut or power line, second-growth oak flat near a cedar swamp (maybe a few last nuts and green vines and leaves), grape or honeysuckle thicket…you get the picture. Set a stand or make a blind on the fringe of a pine, cedar, or honeysuckle thicket. Bucks love to travel a green edge in the woods.

A great bonus now is that most of the rut hunters who crowded the woods in November are long gone. A few of them got their bucks; others have lost interest or had to go back to work. Whatever, the reason, there’s less competition. Hunt Monday through Thursday and you’ll have the woods to yourself most days. Bucks move best on days when there’s less pressure, so you’re in great shape.

In early December, bucks are tired and battered but still running on a last jolt of testosterone. Sometimes a buck makes fresh rubs, so look for them. While bucks generally don’t paw scrapes this late, they often cruise back through creek bottoms and draws where they scraped and rubbed trees a month ago, and hooked up with does. Go back and hunt a stand that you hung in a sign-blazed funnel in early November, you might catch a buck cruising there now.

One cold, still morning in early December, we hiked down into a canyon near the Cimarron River in western Oklahoma and set up on a rocky outcropping. As pink dawn was breaking, my friend Kenny hissed, “Buck in the river.”

I peeked at the deer, an old fellow with a bull chest, thin hips, and a gray face. I hadn’t looked at his rack, but I knew he was a shooter, at least 5 ½ years old.

“Eight pointer, gnarly,” Kenny said while checking him out with his binocular. “He’ll be on our side of the river in a few steps.”

The buck stepped out of the misty river and disappeared into thick brush. He popped out 250 yards away, and I was fixing to try a poke…

I peeked over at Kenny, who worked his horns and grunter with a gleam in his eye.

The buck turned our way and marched in, back hair bristling and face a white halo in the morning sun. My 140-grain bullet drove him into the sandbar, and he never moved again.

Top whitetail scientist Mickey Hellickson conducted an intensive three-year study in Texas on the movements and behaviors of mature bucks. Part of that research project produced groundbreaking research on antler rattling.

“The first weeks of the post-rut, when old bucks cruise for the last hot does, are a good time to keep rattling,” says Hellickson. This was the phase when the researchers rattled up the most mature bucks. Of the 29 bucks that responded to their 51 post-rut rattling sequences in the study, 10 were 5 ½ years old or more, and another 10 were 3 ½ to 4 ½.

Don’t give up on rattling too soon. Here are a few things to keep in mind:

One December day in Kansas, B.J. Clement bowhunted from a ground blind in an old abandoned farmyard where he’d found lots of rubs and scrapes in late October. He saw some young bucks and does, but nothing he wanted to shoot.

To help his Dad out, his son Todd sneaked into the farmyard the next day and stunk up the joint. “I made several mock scrapes, and laid scent trails all through the area with both doe and dominant buck urine,” Todd says.

A few days later, Todd returned and freshened the scrapes and trails.

On the way to his blind the next day, B.J. found the yard torn up with big rubs and fresh scrapes.

Around 4 p.m., B.J. spotted a big rack. The buck marched into the farmyard and thrashed a tree. As the deer worked closer, Clement drew his bow when he could and fired a lethal arrow. The rack scored 181 inches.

Read Next: 7 Deer Hunting Tactics You’ve Never Tried Before But Should

You’ve already read here that in early December adult does that didn’t conceive the first time around cycle into a second estrus. As a bonus, in an agricultural state like Kansas or Iowa where there is good year-round nutrition for deer, a few 7-month-old doe fawns might pop into heat for the first time later on in the month. Whatever the case, these sweet-smelling does can and will draw in bucks.

Back in early November, you probably tried scent lures. But sometimes scent works better the first two weeks of the post-rut. Think about it. During the peak rut, a lot of estrus does mist the woods, and bucks had lots of choices. But now, with only a few estrous does left, the sweet scent of one can bring a buck running to you on a string.

Where legal, lay a doe-in-heat trail into your stand or blind each day. Try doctoring old scrapes with both estrus and tarsal as a challenge to other bucks. Stink up the December woods. The bucks are still out there and moving, and you might get one yet.

#8427. Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote.  “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

The fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#8424. Te Araroa day 23: 500km in, have I found my trail legs yet?

Most of the others left by 7am, but I was a bit slower and wasn’t ready until 7:15. But not to worry, as it’s a running joke that no matter how much later I leave, I’ll catch everyone up soon enough! I could see Annabel up ahead as I left, but the track went into some bushes and I didn’t see her anymore. The mud began pretty much straight out the gate, and at first I was able to avoid it reasonably easily. But it became apparent that I wouldn’t be able to go around it for much longer, so 15 minutes into the day I committed to the mud and put my feet straight in. The first steps are always the worst, and once your feet are already wet and muddy it doesn’t seem so bad anymore.

After a bit of up and down through cow fields, the track went into the bush and I caught up to Lindsay. This was interesting, as I hadn’t passed Annabel, and Annabel hadn’t passed Lindsay either. I figured I must have gone past without realising – maybe she was peeing in a bush or had gone the other way around a tree. Not too long after, there was a steep scramble up with some chains – the first (but not last) chains of TA! I don’t think I used them, but I always enjoy those steep scrambly bits. They use different muscles to the regular walking uphill ones, and it’s a mental puzzle as well as a physical challenge.

At the top of the hill, I found Sinead and Xavier by a helipad. We had read about this helipad in the trail notes, and realised that it must be the same one that someone had posted in the TA Facebook group about using as a campsite one night. Unsurprisingly, that post got a number of comments telling him (more or less politely) that camping on a helipad is a pretty stupid thing to do! Fortunately we were not in need of a camping spot, and continued on. The track continued to go up and down, more or less steeply, more or less muddily, for a while.

Well good, because I sure was wearing some

Eventually I started to hear traffic and surmised I must be getting close to the road. Shortly before the road, there was a steep, wet downhill section that was pretty boggy; and then, hilariously, a wooden bridge over a tiny stream at the bottom. This stream was barely a trickle, while the mud that came before it was at least ankle deep in places. What was the point of the bridge?! The random and pointless boardwalks continued for the last couple of hundred metres to the road. I appreciate the efforts to improve the track, but it really is futile to put a couple of metres of boardwalk in when they are preceded by several kilometres of mud.

At the road, I took a moment to enjoy my favourite hiker trash snack, mayonnaise on crackers. At this point Xavier appeared, and looked disturbed by my choice of topping. ‘Is that… just sauce?!’ My defence: plain crackers are boring, and I’m carrying the mayo for lunch anyway, so why not add more flavour and calories to my snack?

There was a short section of walking along the main road before I turned off onto a smaller one. On the map it was marked as a gravel road, but this was most definitely surfaced. Oh well. There were some decent views in places, and there was a house offering free filtered water. After not too long, I reached the next bit of track. I felt hopeful when I saw that it had steps, and gravel – maybe the next bit wouldn’tbe so muddy? The steps led up to a kauri dieback cleaning station, where I made a valiant attempt to get the mud off my shoes. It wasn’t very successful though – to make a real difference I would have needed running water. Then the track continued uphill on a gravel road/driveway for a bit. It was only 11am, but when I saw a nice grassy patch by the road I decided to stop for lunch. I wasn’t sure where the next flattish and dryish bit of ground would be in the upcoming muddy forest. I was able to have a nice lunch and dry my tent out, but it was getting pretty warm and by the time I got going again I was feeling full, sleepy and unmotivated.

The track went upwards for a bit more before turning off. I knew that this was where the 500km point was, and after missing the 300 and 400km markers I wanted to make sure I did something for this one. There wasn’t a suitable surface to draw on with my pole, so I gathered some small rocks from the road and wrote 500 with them. I took a couple of photos and headed back into the forest. The mud didn’t seem too bad at first, but became similar to the last bit of track. Up, down, up, down, mud, mud, more mud. Some of the downs were extraordinarily steep, too. Earlier in the day I had been able to enjoy the ridiculousness of slogging through mud for fun, but now my enthusiasm was wearing out. Most of the others had passed me when I was having lunch, but at the bottom of a particularly heinous descent I caught Sinead, who was standing in a stream. ‘We’re really close to the campsite now!’ she said. The campsite she referred to was not where we planned to end the day, but a small one on the way at the end of this section of forest. Still, I was happy to hear we were close, and grabbed some water to filter when I got there. I knew there was a stream crossing just at the campsite, so I believed that Sinead was right and it was just around the corner. However after a bit more walking I checked my map and realised it wasn’t the stream crossing I was thinking of, and I was still about a kilometre away.

Eventually, we did arrive at the campsite. I could see Zoe sitting there with Xavier and one or two other people. Zoe set out early that morning as she was racing to meet some friends who were picking her up at the end of the day, and she must have been on a mission as I hadn’t seen her since the morning! She reckoned she got her trail legs all of a sudden – I would like to know if mine are on the way too, because this section was feeling hard!

Also there was Tim, who at first I didn’t recognise, but who I had met at the Ruakaka campsite on the day I arrived. He had been staying with friends and slack packing for a few days. In fact, we had followed him down the beach the previous day – I had seen the hiking pole marks in the sand and the figure in the distance, but not been able to work out who it was.

Lindsay and Anica soon showed up too, but there was no sign of Annabel. We were a bit worried about her, but there wasn’t much to do. At this point, it was about 2:30pm and we still had 7km to do to our intended stop at the Dome cafe. But the temptation to just stay at this perfectly pleasant spot was very strong. I knew I would be annoyed at myself if I stayed, so I washed my shoes and socks in the stream, reapplied my tape, had a snack, and got ready to continue. Someone had said that track conditions improved from this point, and I sure hoped that was the case otherwise it would be a rather late arrival into camp.

Finally some nice, dry track where I can actually appreciate my surroundings

My first view of Rangitoto Island in the Auckland harbour

Signs for improved track conditions sure seemed to be good. Across the road, the track went steeply up on a gravel forestry road. It was steep and hot, but at least not muddy. The gradient continued as the road turned into a track, but it was nowhere near as muddy as the previous sections. I was able to make good time, and when the track took a turn into some native bush, I was able to enjoy it. It was a nice bush track, although still of course rather hilly.

A few kilometres from the end, I reached a trig point. Foolishly, I believed that it would be mostly downhill from here. Boy, was I wrong. There were still at least two substantial hills that just felt never ending. I caught up to Zoe at one point, and finally I came up to a viewpoint where there was a group of day hikers admiring the view, and Tim. I apologised for my smell and asked if it was far to the bottom. It had taken them 20 minutes to get up, which was music to my ears. The track from this point on was all gravelled, with steps. There was one small uphill, which felt big to my tired legs. And finally, I was at the bottom. Zoe’s boyfriend was there, and introduced himself to me, but I was too tired to make intelligent conversation.

The track just after the trig was cool, especially when it was going downhill

There is space for hikers to pitch tents kindly provided by the old Dome cafe, which is being turned into a house. They provide a small tent area, a sheltered kitchen area, and a hot shower! In a bath tub!! Unfortunately there was no curtain or anything around the shower, and it was a glass door out to the deck. So we had to take it in turns and make sure no one was there before heading round. In the past, I probably wouldn’t have been too keen on this arrangement, but I was so tired and desperate for a shower that I didn’t care. Then I was able to sit in a comfy chair and eat the mammoth dinner I had prepared for myself.

Annabel ended up appearing not too long after me, with Lindsay. It turned out she had got lost very early on when the track turned over a fence and she had continued straight on. She ended up not getting further than 1km on the track by 9:30, so it was very impressive that she had managed to catch up! We all agreed that this was one of the toughest days yet. The mud and the relentless up and down were physically challenging and a bit soul-crushing. Anica had actually gotten injured, and she planned to hitch the next day instead of walking.

The floor lit up in the bathroom. Not quite to my taste, but it’s definitely something!

Lindsay and I eat a well-deserved dinner. Photo by Sinéad

The Dome cafe is just off SH1 north of Auckland, and I remember passing the DOC sign on the way up to Kaitaia. We could hear the road noise from where we were camped, and it was strange after a tough and remote-feeling day to be back so close to civilisation. I thought I would fall asleep quickly, but unfortunately the ground was not the flattest and I had managed to pitch my tent such that my head was downhill no matter which way I faced. In the end I shoved my rain jacket under my mat by my head, and was able to sleep.

#8422. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#8421. Range Testing the Sons of Liberty Gunworks Mk 1: Here’s Why Tier-One SOCOM Operators Chose This Carbine

Published Nov 13, 2026 5:19 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

The SOLGW Mk 1 made waves last year for rising to the top during a grueling selection process in which one of our Tier One SOCOM units selected to field it. This 11.5-inch carbine chambered in 5.56 NATO demonstrated the best reliability and performance among its peers.

Not surprisingly, it has since become one of the most desirable AR-platform rifles in the commercial market, though many would-be buyers have balked at its hefty price, which is just shy of three grand.

I’ve spent the last several months running the carbine to see whether the juice is worth the squeeze and you can see it in action in the video here.

My experience with the SOLGW Mk1 has been universally positive. I’ve run it in several configurations, in terms of the optics I’ve mounted on it and with respect to the types of muzzle devices I’ve employed. In all cases, the rifle has run without any glitches.

More impressively, my hands-on time with the rifle has shown how it rises to the occasion when called on to perform different tasks.

For instance, in a multi-gun capacity I ran it with a Vortex 1-10 Gen III Razor LPVO and a Holosun 507C in an offset Area 419 mount. Not only did this setup perform well at distance with the LPVO at 10X, but I was able to quickly transition between far and near targets by rotating the rifle 45 degrees to bring the Holosun’s halo-style reticle rapidly into view.

In another configuration, I ran the rifle with an EOTech holographic sight and 3x magnifier paired with Unity FAST mounts and EOTech’s OGL weapon-mounted laser and IR designator. This setup is much closer to how SOCOM assaulters kit-out the gun. Unsurprisingly, the rifle worked like a charm here too.

A final thing worth noting is the primary muzzle device I used is the Huxwrx Flow 556 Ti, which is also similar to the military’s selection for the Mk1. The rifle has a non-adjustable gas block that balances extremely well with this suppressor, and cuts the gas going back into the shooter’s face to basically zero.

In conjunction with the bolt-carrier group and buffer system, the gas block and suppressor, enhance the SOLGW Mk1’s reliability and soften the recoil impulse in a way that makes the rifle very easy to control.

Reports from the operators who field the rifle indicate that its lethality, performance and reliability are outstanding.

Based on all this, it looks like the Mk 1 delivers in a way that justifies its price, and then some.

#8417. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang said. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

The climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang

#8416. TA Tales: Phase 4 – The Comeback

This post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana. May God’s love, compassion, and mercy fill you, and your family up, then spill over with blessings.

After completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton. With a week of successful walking down, we felt another week of slack packing is maybe overly cautious, but (in my opinion) necessary. You can never be too careful when walking long distances. Taking care of injuries early, and not rushing through the recovery, is essential.

So, our recovery continued along the Waikato River. This is an established walkway for walkers, bikers, and boat racing watchers. Luckily for us, we managed to pick up this section of trail right as the Bridge 2 Bridge races were happening. Slalom skiers, inflatable speed boats, jet skis, and other raceable water craft wizzed past us as we meandered along the paved path.

The trail, post river, takes you through Hamilton, and deposits you just west of town at the Taitua Arboretum. The weather was a bit stormy this week, so in true hiker fashion, we hunkered down, with our new British friends, at The Bank for the afternoon. We played cards, drank $4 pints, and enjoyed each other’s company.

Alice and Matt, our new favorite British couple

Feeling fresh, rejuvenated, and healthy, Maya and I set off from the arboretum. Full packs, flexible walking plan, and high hopes, met by towering native trees, proved a great start to the next leg of our adventure.

The Karamu Walkway is 8.5 km of rolling hills with cool rocks and sheep. Seriously…sheep EVERYWHERE (25,000 to be exactish, according to our friendly trail host). We are just past the lambing season, so all the mama sheep are sheeping about with their lambs. Very cute, except for the fact that all sheep have a severe case of poopy butt, so just don’t look at their rear.

After our time with the sheep, we experienced our first hut. Picture the AMC’s High Mountain hut system, but a bit smaller, no “Croo”, and the huts are included in our trail pass. Mice…nope. Mattresses…yep. Awesome views and everyone staying there is super friendly…absolutely. The climb up and down the Pirongia Traverse was a true test for Maya’s knee, and she left that stretch feeling tired (of course, it was super muddy!), but energized from how great her legs felt. An overall win, and epic section.

Thank goodness for the board walks as you got closer to the hut

Sunset with Dr. Seuss tree from the hut deck

While the sections along the beaches, through farmland, and up and over mountains is why walkers walk, Te Araroa throws some lengthy road walks in there. You know, just to keep you grateful for the time spent not on the road. Walk it, hitch it, whatever. It’s your adventure. Maya and I do put our thumbs out when we can, but if we do end up walking it, we are well prepared with high visibility vests, custom made by Maya herself.

We are currently in Te Kūiti letting some weather pass and planning our next section which includes bike riding and canoe paddling. Sounds like a fun switch up giving our walking legs a rest, and our biking legs/paddling arms, some strength. Looking ahead appears to be pretty dang fun. Stay tuned to find out.

P.S. I have been carrying a kite, and her maiden voyage was at Putaki Shelter. Her name is Putaki, Taki for short. I tried to fly her again at the Waitomo Top 10 Holiday Park, but the wind had a mind of its own that day. Let’s see how long she last.

Hey there, and welcome (: My name is Gillian. Born and raised in Northern Virginia. Veteran, U.S.C.G. Pinto, if we met on the A.T. in 2023. RPCV Samoa. Always ready for a good laugh. A long walk, to take the edge off. That challenge you did not want, but are grateful for. And a keeper, of the faith, all the love, and this thing called courage (“soft front, strong back”).

#8414. Are Deer Dogs Really the Problem with Deer Hunting in the South?

Published Nov 13, 2026 9:41 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Past an old logging gate, a gravel road snakes through a young stand of pine. Meandering through the stand, my truck headlights brighten the back wall of a squat tin building that looks more like an old feed shed than a deer camp. Inside, a makeshift counter holds a logbook for stand locations and check-ins. An aerial map of the property (all 3,000 acres of it) and faded grip-n-grin photos of bucks from past seasons adorn the walls. Every member of the Limestone Creek Hunting Club lives within 20 minutes of here, so there’s no need for actual living quarters. Before this camp house was built, members like my grandfather and father just gathered around an old burn barrel that marked the official rendezvous point. They would meet there first, then decide where to turn the dogs out each morning of the season.

Limestone Creek is just one camp within a patchwork of clubs that are scattered around the Pearl River region of south-central Mississippi. And while a few other surrounding camps also hunt deer with dogs, the Limestone club has clung to this tradition tighter than any, for almost 50 years. In that half century, their dog hunts have become something of an art. The preferred mediums are CB radios, beagles, and old lever guns or pump-action rifles. The featured artist behind these runs is Tim Orders, one of Limestone’s longest tenured members.

On this morning Orders arrives last, in typical fashion, with his blueticks and beagles in tow. While collaring the dogs, he directs everyone to specific posts; road crossings, food plots, and creek bottoms, all named after hunters or the bucks they’d killed there. And while the Limestone club has taken plenty of big bucks over the years, antlers aren’t the reason its members keep coming back. The club’s history,  the shared excitement on successful hunts, and the enduring camp traditions are what dog hunts are really all about.

But for deer hunters who don’t use dogs, and aren’t part of the tradition, it’s easy to be skeptical when you see a battalion of orange vests spread along the roads—possibly near your hunting property. While there are plenty of deer dog hunters who understand boundaries and sensible hunting etiquette, there are plenty who don’t. Those who don’t will surely run through some treestand hunter’s setups. Hunting deer with dogs is currently legal in nine southern states (MS, LA, AR, NC, SC, TN, GA, VA, FL), and when the hounds get to barking it can feel like the end of deer season for everyone else.

But just because dog hunting season begins doesn’t mean that treestand hunters should give up. Here’s what all hunters should understand about dog hunting, and how they can adapt their strategies to still be successful once the hounds hit the woods.

I hunt several areas, both public and private, where deer dog hunters frequent. This year, I rode shotgun with Orders during one of his club’s first hunts of the season to see his deer dog strategies and to learn how to adapt my own hunting around dog hunters. If you’re unfamiliar with hunting deer with dogs, here’s an overview:

If your only experience with deer dogs involves a pack of beagles running through your treestand setup, you probably aren’t a fan of the tradition in general. I’ve been on this end of a dog hunt several times. It can be frustrating. You wake up super early, get to your stand before daylight, only to have a spike run through after sunrise with a pack of beagles trailing behind. It will feel like that spot is burned for the day.

But if you understand how deer react to dogs, you can still be successful during dog season even if you’re not with the deer dog crew.

My grandfather killed his three biggest bucks with dogs in the woods. Two of the three were taken during still hunts when dog hunters on neighboring properties ran deer onto the private ground he was hunting. He’d hunted with dogs before, so he knew the neighbors might run a buck by him.

I know several other hunters who look at dog season as an opportunity to give their hunting season a spark. Land Smathers is a dedicated Mississippi deer hunter who consistently kills mature bucks during dog season, often on public land.

Smathers cited one instance when he noticed that a party of dog hunters convened near some public ground he planned to hunt that morning. His familiarity with this particular ground gave him an idea of where the hunters would likely turn the dogs out, so he decided to quickly set up where he anticipated dogs might drive the deer.

“I knew that area, and there was only one place the deer could go if they were bedded there,” he said. “I slipped down a ridge that dumps into a river bottom where the deer would have to travel or cross the river. Once the dogs cut a track, deer started to funnel through this natural pinch point. I watched several does and a couple small bucks trot through the bottom until a shooter emerged. He came through at 60 yards before I leveled him with a shotgun. The dog hunters weren’t mad that I’d shot him, but they didn’t help me drag him out either.”

Smathers he didn’t always take advantage of dog season throughout his hunting career.

“It used to bother me,” he said. “I’d see a bunch of trucks with dog boxes at the store, and I would turn right around and go home. I finally realized that sulking about it didn’t do any good, so I just learned how to hunt around them, and it’s paid off a few times.”

Smathers’ experience and success in the middle of dog season has made him more empathetic toward the practice, and he sees more hunting opportunities, even with dogs, as a good thing for hunting overall. A lot of hunters grumble that deer hunting with dogs ruins the rest of their season or burns their best spots. It can certainly take a few days for things to return to “normal” in areas that dogs have covered, which is more problematic if you’re hunting small private properties. But the truth is, deer dogs don’t often drive deer completely out of an area.

“We only run dogs during the second season, which typically aligns with our rut,” Orders says. “It seems contrary to most hunters, but that time of year, deer can be so unpredictable anyway. We’ll turn the dogs out in spots where we know a buck is bedded, and if we don’t kill him right away, we’ll give that spot a rest and get a trail cam pic of him back in that same area within a couple days, if not sooner.”

Orders noted that this is especially true during the lockdown phase of the rut, or if there’s a hot doe in the area.

“If the dogs split up a buck and doe, he’ll return shortly to find her again,” Orders says. He also isn’t surprised when a new buck shows up on the property during dog season.

Orders’ style of dog hunting allows him and his club to jump bedded deer that have been heavily pressured. These bucks likely wouldn’t be caught moving during daylight hours otherwise. It’s logical to think that pressure from dogs might make bucks even more nocturnal. But this hasn’t been the case for Smathers, who spends about half his time hunting public land that gets hammered by dog hunters every season. In fact, many of his mature bucks were taken during dog season or shortly after it. Like Orders, he’s noticed that most of the time, bucks will show up shortly after the dogs are gone. While these mature bucks might not daylight in the middle of a food plot, they’re still moving, just in thicker cover, Smathers says.

You don’t have to join a deer dog club to get in on the action. If you’re hunting public ground, and you decide to stick it out when the dog hunters roll up, make sure you’re at a safe distance from other hunters and wearing blaze orange. Then, follow these tips.

Hunt from the ground. If there was ever a time to ditch your treestand or saddle, it’s now. Being stuck in a tree limits your chances of getting a shot. But if you’re hunting from the ground, you can quickly change position as needed.

Cover likely escape routes. Deer prefer the path of least resistance. This is especially true with dogs on their trail. Deer will typically follow their preferred travel routes when jumped. But instead of bed-to-food travel, focus on bed-to-bed travel. The deer are headed for more cover, what’s the quickest route for them? That’s where you need to setup.

Use terrain features. You can use natural pinch points like saddles, creek or river crossings, and ridge systems to your advantage. You can find these with OnX or HuntStand and then fine-tune your setup once you’re there in person. Approach these areas similarly to how you would treestand hunt them but with more flexibility for your setup.

Play the wind. Even though they move based on where the dogs bump them, you can bet deer, especially mature bucks, will still use the wind to their favor. If you’re upwind of the deer, you’re unlikely to get a shot before they detect you.

Hunt the backdoor. Dog hunting crews often refer to an unlikely or underrated travel route that as the “backdoor.” Mature bucks love to sneak out through the backdoor. If you’re hunting a neighboring property and hear the dogs running parallel or even away from you, don’t leave just yet. If a mature buck is bedded near other deer that the dogs jump, they’ll often hang tight until the commotion passes and then slip out opposite or perpendicular to the rest of the deer to head for different cover. If possible, position yourself between “the backdoor” and the next potential bedding area.

Just get out there. If you already adhere to the “you can’t kill them from the couch” approach, this also applies during deer dog season. Adapting your hunting plan is always a better strategy than sitting at home. And if you’re lucky, it might end with a buck heading straight for your setup.

The day I joined Orders for one of Limestone’s hunts, the dogs jumped several does, but no one shot. While Orders isn’t against shooting does this time of year, especially for first timers, there’s an understanding that the club prefers to hold out for bucks. Even though no tags were punched, I still got to hear the dogs bark see all the action of a hunt well run.

READ NEXT: The Vanishing Legacy of Southern Rabbit Hunting

The next day, Orders and his crew did tag a buck and the shot several more before the season ended. With just 14 days (minus a few for bad weather) Limestone’s success rates are a thing to admire, especially when you consider that they only run half days. The club imposes a strict 12 p.m. deadline on itself, as opposed to conducting all day runs like a lot of other hunters might. Letting the property rest is important to their success, which is just one of the many lessons they’ve learned through years of running dogs. One of the key tenets that Orders and his son follow is to drop everything in order to catch dogs before they chase deer off the property. This philosophy not only leaves the club in good standing with surrounding clubs and landowners, it’s even helped them land a few extra spots to run.

Unfortunately, not all deer dog hunters hold themselves to this standard, and most of us can only watch while howling beagles run deer through our setups. But like any hunt, adapting is often the key to finding success. So the next time you hear the dogs jump a deer in your area, stick it out. A big buck could be headed your way.

Adam Moore is a contributor for Outdoor Life. He grew up hunting all the wild game Mississippi has to offer. He now lives in the ever-humid Hattiesburg, Mississippi with his chef-of-a-wife and daughter.

#8409. A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

Deputy leader Lukas Grbac Lackovic spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a new route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential new line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

They climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

They called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing progress, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

One thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

Can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

The two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Currently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

How many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

During the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia…

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive big walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least at the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

The granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

There were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

From there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

All belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

As in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

How much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

The most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a new route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

Your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other big-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.
